cards.b: A classical computer stores bits: 0 or 1. A quantum computer stores qubits, which can be in a superposition of 0 and 1. Linked by entanglement, they might solve some problems (not all) vastly faster. Big claims surround this field. Here is what is solid and what is hype.

Two ordinary bits hold one of four values. Two qubits hold a blend of four values at once, with amplitudes. With n qubits, there are 2ⁿ amplitudes: 300 qubits would need more numbers than there are atoms in the visible universe to describe. This is the reason a classical computer cannot easily simulate a big quantum one.

Richard Feynman (1981) pointed out that to simulate quantum nature efficiently, you need a computer that is itself quantum. David Deutsch (1985) gave the first formal model.

A common myth says a quantum computer tries every answer at the same time. Measuring gives just one random result. The art is to design steps so that wrong answers cancel and the right one adds up, using interference.

• Shor (1994): factors large numbers in a number of steps that grows only polynomially. Classical methods grow far faster. It would break the RSA and elliptic-curve encryption used online.
  • Grover (1996): searches an unsorted list of N items in about √N steps rather than N: a speed-up, but only a square-root one.
  • Simulation of molecules and materials: possibly the most useful near-term target.

Qubit types: superconducting circuits (Google, IBM), trapped ions (Quantinuum, IonQ), neutral atoms, photons, and spins in silicon. Google's 2019 Sycamore (53 qubits) claimed "quantum supremacy": a task in 200 seconds that they estimated would take a supercomputer 10,000 years. IBM disputed this, and later classical methods narrowed the gap. The task had no practical use. In December 2024 Google's Willow chip (105 qubits) showed that adding qubits could reduce errors, a key milestone for error correction.

Qubits are fragile: decoherence and noisy gates cause errors in roughly one in a thousand steps at best. Quantum error correction combines many physical qubits into one reliable "logical qubit". A 2025 estimate by Craig Gidney (Google) suggested breaking RSA-2048 might need fewer than one million noisy qubits running for about a week, a big reduction from older estimates, but today's machines have hundreds to a few thousand qubits, not millions.

Machines exist and are improving fast, but, to the best of public knowledge, they have not yet beaten classical computers at a commercially useful task by a clear margin. Cryptographically relevant machines are not expected for years; timelines vary widely and are uncertain.

• "It tries all answers at once." It uses interference to steer.
  • "It will replace your laptop." It helps only with special problems.
  • "It can break all encryption tomorrow." Not yet; and new post-quantum codes exist.

In April 2025 the Bengaluru start-up QpiAI launched QpiAI-Indus, billed as India's first full-stack 25-qubit superconducting quantum computer. A larger machine has been announced. India's National Quantum Mission (approved April 2023) sets a goal of 50 to 1,000 physical qubits over eight years. TIFR and IISc are building superconducting qubits; the IISc-led hub focuses on computing.

• Qubits use superposition and entanglement; algorithms use interference.
  • Shor (1994) threatens RSA; Grover (1996) gives a square-root speed-up.
  • Error correction is the main hurdle; practical advantage is not yet broad (as of 2026).

Think about it

  1. Why does measuring a quantum computer give only one answer?
  2. Why can 300 qubits not be simulated classically?
